ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a transistor common-emitter amplifier circuit; R1 and R2 form the base bias, R3 is in the collector circuit, and the output is coupled through C2; below the emitter, a resistor R4 is connected to ground, and capacitor CE is connected in parallel with R4, serving as the emitter bypass capacitor. Reasoning: When CE is open-circuited, the AC small signal no longer bypasses R4 through CE; R4 will appear in the emitter AC path, forming stronger emitter negative feedback/emitter degeneration and increasing the equivalent emitter resistance, so the magnitude of the voltage gain becomes smaller.

raw_record.question_text: In the circuit shown in the figure, what happens to the amplification when capacitor \(C_E\) is disconnected?

method.method_draft: First read the circuit structure from the image: CE is connected in parallel with the emitter resistor R4. Then use the text condition that CE is disconnected. In the AC small-signal model, removing CE means R4 is no longer bypassed and appears in the emitter path. The effective emitter resistance increases, so the voltage gain magnitude becomes smaller. Conclude that the amplification decreases.

planner_metadata.image_role: Identify the diagram as a common-emitter transistor amplifier: input is coupled through C1 to the base, output is coupled through C2 from the collector, R3 is the collector resistor, R4 is in the emitter lead, and CE is drawn in parallel with R4 from emitter to ground.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the prompt’s requested change: capacitor CE is disconnected, and determine the resulting change in amplification.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: For midband AC analysis, a bypass capacitor across the emitter resistor makes the emitter nearly AC-grounded; without the bypass capacitor, the emitter resistor remains in the AC signal path. Common-emitter gain magnitude is roughly Rc/re when bypassed, but roughly Rc/(re+R4 or its AC equivalent contribution) when unbypassed, so the denominator increases.

method.method_draft: Describe the image as a common-emitter amplifier where CE normally bypasses the emitter resistor R4 for AC signals. Apply the text condition: disconnecting CE removes this bypass. Then reason qualitatively that signal current through R4 develops an AC emitter voltage that opposes changes in base-emitter voltage, adding negative feedback. More negative feedback means smaller amplification, so the amplification decreases.
method.CoT_raw:
Image description: The attached circuit is a transistor common-emitter amplifier. The input is coupled through C1 to the base, R1 and R2 form a base bias divider, R3 is connected in the collector path to UCC, and the output is coupled through C2 from the collector. The emitter has resistor R4 to ground, and capacitor CE is connected in parallel with R4 as an emitter bypass capacitor.
Reasoning: In normal operation, CE bypasses R4 for AC signals, reducing AC emitter degeneration and increasing voltage gain. If CE is disconnected, the AC signal current must pass through R4, producing an AC voltage at the emitter. This emitter voltage opposes changes in the base-emitter voltage, introducing negative feedback. Greater negative feedback reduces the amplifier gain, so the amplification decreases.

planner_metadata.image_role: Observe that the transistor stage has an emitter resistor R4 to ground and a capacitor CE shunting that resistor, while the signal enters the base through C1 and exits the collector through C2, indicating a bypassed-emitter common-emitter amplifier.

planner_metadata.knowledge_role: An unbypassed emitter resistor produces emitter degeneration: when collector/emitter current changes with the input signal, the emitter voltage also changes, reducing the base-emitter signal variation. This negative feedback lowers voltage amplification. A connected CE suppresses this AC feedback by shorting R4 for signal frequencies.
